newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels announce advances in north and south.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels announce advances in north and south.

text.p: Zairean rebels said on Tuesday they had seized a port in the southern mining region of Shaba and would soon capture the northeastern city of Kisangani, a government stronghold on the Zaire river.
The French government, which backs ailing president Mobutu Sese Seko, denounced what it called a "conspiracy of silence" over Zaire and called for urgent humanitarian intervention in the country.
At rebel headquarters in the eastern city of Goma, rebel spokesman Raphael Ngenda said clashes between rebel and government forces had begun around Kisangani, capital of northeast Zaire.
Rebel radio said fighters of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) were within 10 km (six miles) of Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city.
But a regional military source told Reuters on Tuesday the closest rebel unit was still 40 km (25 miles) from Kisangani and he expected fighting for the city to start in about 48 hours.
The radio said that on Sunday the rebels captured the port town of Moba on Lake Tanganyika, some 750 km (470 miles) to the south in the copper and cobalt-mining region of Shaba.
France, which has championed foreign intervention in Zaire since the start of the conflict last October, once again pleaded for the world community to act.

"The humanitarian situation in Zaire is tragic. No one can ignore it any longer. No one can remain indifferent," French government spokesman Alain Lamassoure quoted President Jacques Chirac as saying.
"We have to ask if there is not a sort of conspiracy of silence."

"France appeals solemnly to the international community to take responsibility by exerting the necessary pressure to obtain a ceasefire and to implement urgently needed humanitarian intervention," Chirac was quoted as telling a cabinet meeting.

France backs Mobutu, 66, who has autocratically presided over the declining fortunes of Zaire for 31 years. After cancer surgery last August he has spent most of his time in Europe and is now at his villa on the French Riviera.
Lamassoure said the French government strongly supported proposals by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan for an international humanitarian intervention force. The plan has received little backing.

Emergency Humanitarian Aid Minister Xavier Emmanuelli, just back from Zaire, told the cabinet the refugee situation was "very sombre" and proposed that France should launch its own mini-airlift while waiting for wider international support.
Rebel radio said the fall of Kisangani, the base for an ineffective mercenary-backed government counter-offensive, was imminent and repeated a March 13 deadline for Zaire soldiers to give up arms.

"Most of the people have fled Kisangani while soldiers are stealing, raping and killing," it said. Zaire's defence ministry says rebels are within 100 km (60 miles) to the north and northeast of the city and 50 km (30 miles) to the southeast.
The government and rebels have attached huge symbolic value to Kisangani. It is at the end of the navigable stretch of the Zaire river flowing down to the Zairean capital Kinshasa.
Military analysts say should Kisangani fall, Shaba province and diamond-rich Kasai could follow in a domino effect.
The AFDL, led by veteran guerrilla Laurent Kabila, has taken at least a sixth of the third largest country in Africa.
Bizima Karaha, rebel foreign affairs commissioner, said on Tuesday the AFDL had no intention to attack Ubundu town, where 40,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees fled over the weekend.
He said the rebels gave the international community every chance to set up a humanitarian corridor to allow refugees to head home. Ubundu is 100 km (60 miles) southeast of Kisangani.
The U.N. refugee agency said on Tuesday that about 400,000 refugees were unaccounted for in Zaire. Some of those refugees who had been found were so weak they could barely walk.
